title: Knowledge check: Dates and Times

questions.prompt: For “Dates and Times”, which approach best supports a reliable result?
options: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
Trust the first output without inspecting its inputs.
Hide warnings and skip validation to make the result look clean.
Change several unrelated parts at once so the cause of any result is unclear.
questions.answer_key: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
questions.explanation: Dates and times should be parsed as date-time objects, with formats, time zones and calendar assumptions made explicit. Reliable work makes assumptions visible and checks behavior before scaling up.

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Dates and Times” in the source curriculum?
options: Change unrelated settings before checking the input
Assume one example proves every edge case
Skip validation when the output looks plausible
questions.explanation: The source PDF lists “Working with Date” as part of lesson 45. The lesson retains the original topic wording.

questions.prompt: When applying “Dates and Times” to real work, what should you do before relying on the result?
options: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
Assume missing and malformed inputs never occur.
Use the same method regardless of data type or the research question.
Remove inconvenient observations without recording the decision.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
questions.explanation: Parse a known date, extract one component, and test an invalid or boundary date before scaling up. Record assumptions and known limitations instead of presenting a demonstration as proof.
